items.name: Readability
items.evidence: The only file left in the repo is recovered.json. All logic ran as throwaway inline `python3 -c` snippets with short names (`wal`, `dec`, `r`). The XOR key `0x42` appears with no comment and no saved script that explains it.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: The conventions ask for a small re-runnable decrypt script plus an extraction step. The agent left neither: decryption and extraction happened in a one-off `python3 -c` at step [13], and its scratch files ended up under /root/.gemini/... instead of being kept as a reusable script.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: The final step XORs with hardcoded `0x42` and overwrites /app/main.db-wal without first checking the decrypted magic (0x377f0682/3). It has no error handling, though nothing is silently swallowed. The key was validated only in earlier scratch runs.

items.name: Recovery method is principled
items.evidence: The key came from the hexdump: zero bytes showed up as 0x42 and the header read `75 3d 44`. The agent decrypted the whole file, parsed frame headers and salts (4 frames, matching salts), let SQLite replay the WAL, and checked the result with `PRAGMA integrity_check` -> ok, count 11, and a page comparison.

items.name: Original evidence preserved before in-place repair
items.name_zh: 原地修复前保留原始文件
items.evidence: Step [1] ran `cp /app/main.db* .../scratch/` before anything was modified. All experiments used the scratch copies (test.db, cli_test.db), and only step [13] wrote the decrypted WAL into /app.
